faqs.q: An iguana was seen near our Stuart dock — should we be worried?
faqs.a: Aware, not worried. Martin County is report-level iguana country: sightings occur, FWC tracks them, and established breeding colonies like South Florida's are not the local picture. Photograph the animal, report it to FWC's exotic species program, and check your seawall for burrowing. If an iguana settles on your property, humane removal there is lawful — and relocation is prohibited everywhere in Florida — but one photographed lizard does not justify a colony-management contract, and we will not sell you one.

Stuart.wildlife_intro:
Stuart, the Sailfish Capital, is the Treasure Coast's historic core — a walkable downtown on the St. Lucie River, the old Roosevelt Bridge, Port Salerno's working waterfront and Manatee Pocket, and neighborhoods from Jensen's edge to the South Fork. The river system runs the wildlife: raccoons on every dock, roof rats in the waterfront palms, opossums and armadillos inland, and iguana sightings that sit squarely in the Treasure Coast's report-level category — documented, FWC-notified, not inflated into a colony scare.

Port Salerno's fishing fleet means Stuart gets commercial waterfront work — dock and shed raccoons, gull and pigeon pressure at the fish houses (protected species handled by deterrence) — alongside residential craft. Our inspections cover the dock boxes and boathouse lofts homeowners forget. For iguana reports, we verify, document, and refer; a confirmed resident animal on your property can be removed lawfully and never released, and we will tell you which situation you actually have.

faqs.q: Are squirrels in a Jensen Beach attic always a removal job?
faqs.a: Our squirrel work is for the eastern gray squirrel only — it is the attic species here. Fox squirrels may not be taken or pursued in Florida, and a large, slow squirrel on the ground is an identification stop, not a booking, especially in southwest Florida where the Big Cypress fox squirrel is State Threatened. For gray squirrels, our crew uses one-way exclusion and seals the roofline so the animals leave and cannot return.

Jensen Beach.wildlife_intro:
In Jensen Beach, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — small coastal cities, riverfront suburbs, and inland rural and equestrian land — and features such as St. Lucie River, Jonathan Dickinson State Park, Savannas Preserve, Indian River Lagoon keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Jensen Beach jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

faqs.q: Coyotes are seen in our Palm City neighborhood — what should residents do?
faqs.a: Respect them and remove the subsidies. Coyotes in Martin County hunt rodents and rabbits along the preserve edges and are not a trapping service we sell as a subscription; conflicts concentrate where pets roam free at night or food sits out. Keep cats in, walk dogs leashed at dawn and dusk, secure trash, and haze a bold coyote — noise, arms up, no approach. A coyote that has lost its fear and threatens people is an FWC conversation; a healthy one trotting the fairway at sunrise is the ecosystem working.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Hobe Sound?
faqs.a: Hobe Sound quotes are small-town careful: one inspection, burrows sorted, roofline mapped, written figure — with protected-species identification treated as part of the visit's value, not a billable removal.

faqs.q: A big tortoise burrow is under my Hobe Sound fence line — options?
faqs.a: Coexistence is the usual answer, and it is easy here: gopher tortoises in Jonathan Dickinson's orbit are everywhere, their burrows are protected, and a fence-line burrow typically costs a homeowner nothing but a mowing detour. Keep dogs from digging at it, never block or fill it, and if a project truly requires work within 25 feet, the path is an FWC permit with an Authorized Agent relocating the tortoise. We identify and mark; the permit world belongs to FWC, and in Hobe Sound most residents end up fond of the tenant.

Hobe Sound service is low-key and precise, like the town. Scrub-edge homes get tortoise-first burrow identification as a reflex. Beachside work respects turtle season in scheduling and lighting conversations. Our removal list is handled with trapping and exclusion under your authorization, traps checked daily, and the park's residents — jays, tortoises, indigos — are identification-and-referral only, every time, no exceptions sold.

faqs.q: What should I do about armadillo digging in Indiantown?
faqs.a: Nine-banded armadillos dig for grubs and earthworms in lawns and flower beds, and they are common throughout most of Florida, including Indiantown. A live-trapped armadillo may be released on-site, or released within the same county on 40 or more contiguous acres with the landowner's written permission, within 24 hours — those are the Florida rules, and we follow them. We also talk through fencing and grub management, because trapping alone rarely ends digging in good habitat.
